content: Case studies represent one of several methodologies employed in social science research. Other methods include experiments, surveys, historical analyses, and the examination of archival data (Yin, 2003). Unlike approaches that rely on large sample sizes and rigid protocols to analyze a limited number of variables, case study methods focus on an in-depth, longitudinal investigation of a single instance or event, referred to as a case. This approach provides a systematic framework for observing events, collecting data, analyzing information, and reporting findings. Through this process, researchers can develop a more nuanced understanding of why a particular instance occurred as it did and identify areas for further, more extensive research. Case studies are particularly useful for both generating and testing hypotheses (Flyvbjerg, 2006). Yin (2002) defines case study research as a strategic methodology, an empirical inquiry that examines a phenomenon within its real-life context. This type of research can involve single or multiple case studies, incorporate quantitative evidence, rely on multiple sources of data, and benefit from the prior development of theoretical propositions. Yin emphasizes that case studies should not be conflated with qualitative research, as they can be based on a combination of both quantitative and qualitative evidence. Single-subject research provides the statistical framework for drawing inferences from quantitative case study data. Lamnek (2005) further supports this view, describing the case study as a research approach that bridges concrete data collection techniques and methodological paradigms. When selecting a case for a case study, researchers often employ information-oriented sampling rather than random sampling (Flyvbjerg, 2006). This is because typical or average cases often lack the richness of information that extreme or atypical cases can provide. Extreme or atypical cases reveal more information by activating fundamental mechanisms and involving more actors in the situation under study. From both an understanding-oriented and action-oriented perspective, it is often more critical to uncover the deeper causes behind a problem and its consequences than to merely describe the symptoms of the problem and their frequency. Random samples, which prioritize representativeness, rarely yield such insights. Instead, selecting a few cases based on their validity is more appropriate. Three types of information-oriented cases can be distinguished: extreme or deviant cases, critical cases, and paradigmatic cases. A critical case is strategically significant in relation to a general problem. For example, an occupational medicine clinic investigating whether exposure to organic solvents causes brain damage might strategically select a single workplace where all safety regulations regarding cleanliness, air quality, and other factors are strictly adhered to. This model enterprise becomes a critical case: if brain damage related to organic solvents is found in this facility, it is likely to exist in other enterprises with less stringent safety measures. This type of strategic sampling can save both time and resources in researching a given problem. Another example of critical case sampling is the strategic selection of lead and feather to test whether different objects fall at the same velocity. A paradigmatic case serves as an exemplar or prototype. Thomas Kuhn demonstrated that the foundational skills and practices of natural scientists are organized around exemplars or paradigms, which play a critical role in the scientific process. Similarly, scholars like Clifford Geertz and Michel Foucault have structured their research around specific cultural paradigms. For Geertz, the deep play of the Balinese cockfight served as a paradigm, while for Foucault, European prisons and the Panopticon were paradigmatic examples. These instances highlight broader characteristics of the societies or issues in question. Kuhn also showed that scientific paradigms cannot be reduced to rules or theories, as there is no predictive theory for how predictive theories emerge. Scientific activity is judged as good science based on its alignment with one or more exemplars, which serve as practical prototypes of high-quality scientific work. A paradigmatic case of how scientists conduct science functions as such a prototype, serving as a reference point and potentially founding schools of thought. The case study is particularly effective for generalizing through falsification, a concept introduced by Karl Popper as part of critical reflexivity (Flyvbjerg, 2006). Falsification is one of the most rigorous tests for a scientific proposition: if a single observation contradicts the proposition, it is considered invalid and must be revised or rejected. Popper famously used the example All swans are white, proposing that the observation of a single black swan would falsify this proposition, thereby stimulating further investigations and theory-building. Case studies are well-suited for identifying black swans due to their in-depth approach, as what initially appears to be white often turns out to be black upon closer examination. For instance, Galileo's rejection of Aristotle's law of gravity was based on a case study selected through information-oriented sampling rather than random sampling. This rejection was primarily conceptual and later supported by practical experiments. Despite the clarity of these experiments in hindsight, Aristotle's incorrect view of gravity dominated scientific inquiry for nearly two millennia before being falsified. Galileo's experimental reasoning was as follows: if two objects of the same weight are released from the same height simultaneously, they will hit the ground at the same time, having fallen at the same speed. If the two objects are then combined into one, this new object will have double the weight and, according to the Aristotelian view, should fall faster than the two individual objects. This conclusion seemed contradictory to Galileo, leading him to eliminate weight as a determinant of acceleration in free fall. Galileo's experimentalism did not involve a large random sample of trials but rather a single experiment—a case study. His view continued to face skepticism, and the Aristotelian view was not definitively rejected until the invention of the air pump, which enabled the ultimate experiment: a coin or piece of lead falling at the same speed as a feather in a vacuum tube. This experiment conclusively disproved Aristotle's view. Notably, the matter was resolved through an individual case due to the strategic selection of extremes, such as metal and feather. This critical case demonstrated that if Galileo's thesis held for these materials, it could be expected to apply to a wide range of materials. Random and large samples were never part of the process. By strategically selecting cases in this manner, researchers can arrive at case studies that allow for generalization. As a distinct research approach, the use of case studies originated in the early 20th century. The Oxford English Dictionary traces the term case study back to 1934, following the establishment of the concept of a case history in medicine. The use of case studies to develop new theories in social sciences was further advanced by sociologists Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss, who introduced their research method, grounded theory, in 1967. The popularity of case studies for testing hypotheses has grown only in recent decades. One area where case studies have gained traction is education, particularly in educational evaluation. Prominent scholars in educational case studies include Robert Stake and Jan Nespor. Case studies have also been used as a teaching method and as part of professional development, especially in business and legal education. The problem-based learning (PBL) movement is one such example. In non-business education and professional development, case studies are often referred to as critical incidents (see David Tripp for references). When the Harvard Business School was established, the faculty quickly realized that there were no textbooks suitable for a graduate program in business. Their initial solution was to interview leading business practitioners and write detailed accounts of their practices. However, the professors could not present these cases as models to emulate, as there were no criteria for determining what would succeed or fail. Instead, students were instructed to read the cases, come to class prepared to discuss them, and offer recommendations for appropriate courses of action. This model remains in use today.
